practices: Slowly look around your space, letting your gaze land on neutral or pleasant objects. Name them silently: lamp, tree, blue cup.
Name 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you can touch, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.
Stand with feet hip-width apart. Shift weight forward/back, side to side. Visualize roots growing from your feet into the earth.
Feel where your body meets the chair or floor. Notice the weight of your body being held by the surface beneath you.
Place one hand on heart, one on belly. Self-hold while breathing slowly. Feel the warmth and containment of your own touch.
Cross arms, tuck hands under opposite armpits, cross ankles, tuck chin. Hold 30-60 seconds to feel contained.
One palm on forehead, one on heart. Alternate attention between the hands, then feel from inside the body what each hand senses.
Walk slowly, feeling each foot contact the ground. Notice the roll from heel to toe.
Inhale 4 counts, exhale 4 counts through the nose. Repeat 5-10 times.
Inhale through nose, exhale through pursed lips like blowing out a candle. Make exhales longer than inhales.
Inhale deeply, exhale with a low 'vooooo' sound, feeling vibrations in chest. Repeat 3-5 times.
Inhale, then hum on the exhale. Notice vibrations in chest, throat, face. Adjust pitch to find what soothes.
As you exhale, play with sounds: 'ahhhh,' 'psssss,' 'hmm.' Feel the vibration. Empty until the sound is gone.
Place hands on sides of ribs. Gently squeeze on exhale, release on inhale.
Lie down, hand on chest, hand on belly. Breathe so only the belly hand moves.
Cross arms over chest, hands on collarbones. Alternate tapping left-right-left-right slowly while breathing.
Squeeze opposite arms, experimenting with pressure and speed. Feel the contrast between squeezed and released.
Place palms on tops of thighs near hips. Press in, then glide down toward knees on exhale.
Wrap arms around yourself, gently sway side to side.
Lightly brush your own arms, legs, or face with fingertips.
Tense entire body on inhale, release completely on exhale.
Stand or sit with feet grounded. Let hands, arms, legs tremble naturally without forcing. Rest and notice after.
Allow gentle shaking to travel from hands up through shoulders, into torso, down through legs. Let it be involuntary.
On all fours, inhale arch back (cow), exhale round spine (cat). Connect breath to movement.
Kneel, toes together, knees apart, fold forward resting torso between thighs. Arms extended or by sides.
Lie with hips against wall, legs extended up. Rest arms comfortably. Stay 5-20 minutes.
Lie on back, pull knees toward chest, then gently toward shoulders. Hold 30 seconds.
Stand, reach both arms up as if grabbing stars from the night sky. Keep reaching until arms tire, then release slowly.
Curl into a tight ball starting from chest inward. Notice breath. Feel if it's safe or unsafe. Slowly unfurl.
Sit and gently rock pelvis forward and back, finding stability through movement.
Gentle rotations, side bends, and movements to mobilize back, ribs, neck, shoulders.
Use a tennis ball or foam roller against wall/floor to release shoulder/neck tension.
Scan body for one area of tension and one neutral area. Slowly pendulate attention between them.
Close fist tightly. Open slowly, noticing the space between each finger. Close again. Observe the space.
Draw an outline of your body and mark where you feel sensations, tension, or emotions.
Close eyes. Notice heartbeat, temperature, muscle tension, digestive feelings, breath rhythm.
Sit comfortably, elbows on knees, cup palms over eyes without pressing. Breathe in the darkness for 3 breaths.
Focus on one object, then soften gaze until it blurs. Close eyes, wait for body to relax, reopen.
Put on music and let your body find its natural rhythm. Dance without choreography.
Notice how you're feeling, then move your body as if you felt the opposite. Exaggerate the shift.
Let yourself sigh, groan, hum, or make whatever sound your body wants to release.
Reach up and 'grab' imaginary stars, bringing them down to different parts of your body.
Crawl like a bear, shake like a dog, stretch like a cat, roll like an otter.
Remember a time someone was kind to you. Notice how your body recalls it -- sensations, warmth, expansion.
Imagine a place where you feel completely safe. Feel it in your body -- temperature, posture, breath.
Imagine roots extending from your spine or feet deep into the earth, drawing up stability.
Visualize releasing weight or tension without actually moving. Let the image facilitate the shift.
Run cool water over your wrists or hold a cold water bottle. Notice temperature change.
Stand barefoot on grass, dirt, or concrete. Feel the texture, temperature, connection to earth.
Sip room temperature water or warm tea slowly. Notice scent, taste, warmth, movement down throat.
Hold an ice cube briefly. Intense sensation brings you immediately to present moment.
Tense feet on inhale, release on exhale. Move up through legs, belly, chest, arms, face.
When overwhelmed, touch into a sensation for just 2-3 seconds, then resource with a butterfly hug or safe memory. Repeat.
Extend arms to sides, push against a wall or doorframe. Feel your edges, your 'no,' your container.
Hand on heart, hand on belly, back against wall. Feel spine supported, core aligned.
niceSelf: Wrap both hands around a warm ceramic mug. Feel the heat seep into your palms, then spread up your forearms.
Keep two spoons in the freezer. Press the curved backs gently against closed eyelids for 30 seconds. Feel the rush of warmth returning.
Soak a washcloth in hot water, wring out, drape over your entire face. Breathe the steam until it cools.
Run an ice cube slowly along your inner wrist, up to the elbow crease, down to the palm. Follow the melt water with your eyes.
At the end of your shower, turn water to cool for 30 seconds on the back of your neck. Then warm again. Repeat once.
Fill a sock with rice, microwave 1-2 minutes. Place on belly, chest, or feet. Mold it to your contours like a weighted companion.
Keep a smooth stone in the fridge. Hold it when anxious, feeling the temperature neutralize with your body heat.
Run a silk scarf or smooth fabric slowly across your forearm, watching the skin goosebump in its wake. Reverse direction.
Find something velvet. Rub it between thumb and fingers, then press to your cheek. Notice the directional nap.
Use a dry brush to stroke your arm from shoulder to wrist, then back up. Count the bristle sensations.
Walk slowly across different surfaces in your home: tile, wood, carpet, bathmat. Name the texture of each to yourself.
Fold a heavy quilt into a square and place just on your chest or belly while lying down.
Stroke a pet slowly with the fur growth, then against. If no pet, use a plush toy or fuzzy blanket with the same attention.
Fill a bowl with dry rice. Submerge your hand, close fist, release, letting grains fall through fingers. Listen to the sound.
Keep clay or playdough near your desk. When stressed, squeeze until your hand tires, then slowly release finger by finger.
Put a drop of essential oil or perfume on a cotton ball. Keep in a sealed bag. When needed, open and inhale deeply three times.
Hold whole coffee beans in your palm. Crush one between fingers, inhale the fresh burst.
Zest a lemon or orange, then run your fingernail under the oily peel. Press that finger to your wrist pulse point.
Find your oldest book. Open to the middle pages, bury your nose, inhale the vanilla-like scent of lignin decay.
Sharpen a wooden pencil with a hand sharpener. Cup the shavings, inhale the cedar/graphite mix.
If it's raining, step outside briefly. If not, wet a hot pan slightly and inhale the steam -- petrichor, the smell of rain.
If you have a tuning fork, strike it and press the base to your sternum. Feel the resonance in your chest cavity.
Wet your finger and run it around the rim of a wine glass until it sings. Hold the note, feel the vibration in your hand.
Use a soft makeup brush on your own forearm slowly, listening to the whisper sound.
Instead of generic rain sounds, search for brown noise or pink noise -- deeper, womb-like frequencies. Notice which your body prefers.
Ring a small bell or chime. Listen until you can no longer hear it, even the memory of it. Count how long that takes.
Lie on your side in a quiet room. Place your hand under your ear, pressing gently. Listen to your pulse until it becomes a rhythm.
Hum a steady note. Place fingers on your cheekbones, then collarbone, then sternum. Feel where the vibration lives strongest.
Place a square of dark chocolate on your tongue. Don't chew. Let it melt completely, noticing the stages: bitter, creamy, sweet.
Take a teaspoon of raw honey. Let it sit on your tongue until it warms and thins. Swallow slowly.
Place a single flaky sea salt crystal on your tongue. Press it to the roof of your mouth. Let it dissolve grain by grain.
Freeze grapes. Take one, let it warm slightly in your mouth, then bite slowly, feeling the ice crystals crack.
Heat milk with a grating of fresh nutmeg. Sip from a small cup, holding the warmth in your mouth before swallowing.
Steep chamomile or hibiscus. Watch the color bloom in the water like ink. Don't stir. Let it happen on its own time.
Buy dried licorice root sticks. Chew the end until soft, sucking the sweet, earthy extract.
Light a candle in a dark room. Stare at the flame without blinking as long as possible. Close eyes and watch the afterimage.
Hang a prism in a sunny window. Lie on the floor and let the moving rainbows fall across your face and body.
Lie on your back outside. Find one cloud. Watch it morph, naming the shapes until it dissolves entirely.
Find a bright star. Stare at it until you see it twinkle. Confirm to yourself: light is reaching my eye from light-years away.
Find a wall or object with a gradient. Stare at the transition point between two colors until the boundary blurs.
Use a weighted eye pillow or rice sock over eyes. Open eyes under the darkness. See the phosphenes -- stars, colors, patterns.
Lie on the edge of your bed. Roll yourself tightly in the sheet like a burrito. Lie still, feeling the pressure. Slowly unroll.
Sit against a wall, thighs parallel to floor. Balance a book on your head. Focus on the weight and alignment.
Lie on the floor, extend arms and legs as wide as possible. Feel yourself occupying space. Wiggle fingers and toes at the edges.
Sit in a chair. Imagine it is dissolving. You are floating, held only by your own posture. Adjust micro-muscles.
Make shadow puppets on a wall. Make them interact with your actual body shadow.
Stare at your own eyes in a mirror for 3 minutes. Notice when your face becomes unfamiliar, then familiar again.
Drape a blanket over two chairs. Crawl inside with a pillow. Let the fabric create a sensory deprivation chamber for 10 minutes.
Clear a closet floor. Add pillow, blanket, book light. Sit inside with door cracked. Feel the containment of small spaces.
Run the shower hot, close the door, sit on the floor outside the spray. Let the steam fill the room. Breathe the humidity.
If you have a car, recline the passenger seat. Bring a pillow and blanket. Listen to rain on the roof or the engine cooling.
Clear a windowsill wide enough to sit. Add cushion. Sit with legs dangling inside, looking out -- inside and outside simultaneously.
Before bed, warm oil between palms. Massage each toe, the arch, the heel. Pull each toe gently. Put on socks, sleep.
Run cold water over your inner wrists for 60 seconds before bed. Lowers body temperature, signals sleep.
Mix water with a few drops of lavender or cedar in a spray bottle. Mist your pillowcase 10 minutes before sleep.
niceOther: Return a shopping cart for someone who just unloaded it, without making eye contact or waiting for thanks.
Pick up three pieces of litter on your block that aren't yours. No one sees you do it. The street is just cleaner tomorrow.
If you're getting off an elevator before someone, press their floor button before they reach the panel. Don't mention it.
Hold a door, then look away so the person doesn't feel pressured to rush or thank you.
If you see a parking meter with time expiring, drop a quarter in. Leave no note.
Slip a handwritten note inside a library book before returning it: 'You chose well. This one matters.'
If a neighbor's mailbox flag is still up after dark, close it for them.
Throw away someone's obviously dead porch plant when they're not home. Replace it with nothing. Just remove the sadness.
If you see a dropped shopping list in a grocery store, buy one item from it and leave it at customer service with the list.
Lift someone's windshield wipers off their windshield if snow is coming. They'll never know who prepared them.
Tell a stranger exactly what you like about them: a specific compliment. Then leave. No conversation.
Read a cashier's name tag. Say their name once, genuinely: 'Thanks, Marcus.' Watch them remember they have a name today.
When someone is searching for words, don't fill the silence. Count to five in your head. Let them find their own sentence.
At self-checkout, start bagging for the person next to you without asking. Say 'I have time' if they protest.
If someone asks you a question while you're wearing headphones, remove them completely before answering. Show them the whole attention.
Sit on your stoop at a consistent time. Wave to the same passersby until they wave back. Then just nod. Then just exist together.
Carry dog treats. Ask 'Can I give your dog a treat?' before asking the dog's name. The human matters first.
See someone struggling to take a selfie or group photo? Offer to take it. Take three. Hand back the phone. Walk away.
If someone is carrying something heavy, don't ask if they need help. Just open the door and stand there holding it.
If a car stops for you at a crosswalk, walk slightly faster than necessary. Show them their kindness wasn't wasted.
Write a letter to a specific stranger you observed. Don't deliver it. The writing was the connection.
Leave a pressed flower or note in a used book at a bookstore: 'I loved this part too.' No signature.
Write 'You look like you're having a hard day. It's okay.' on a napkin. Leave it on a table where someone just was.
If you see a car with an out-of-state plate, leave a note: 'Welcome. This city is glad you're here.' No contact info.
On the back of your library receipt, write a book recommendation for the next person. Leave it in the book drop.
Tape a small drawing or poem to a public trash can. 'Even this is worthy of decoration.' Signed, Anonymous.
Leave a book you loved on a bench with a note: 'Free. Finished. Yours now.' Don't wait to see who takes it.
Mail a postcard to a random address in your city: 'Hope your Tuesday was okay. -- A neighbor.' No return address.
Write a haiku on the back of a receipt. Leave it in the shopping cart.
In a public restroom, leave a small note on the mirror edge: 'You look like someone who tries hard. I see you.'
When someone tells you something mundane, repeat their exact words back later. They'll feel catalogued, cared for.
Ask three coworkers their birthdays. Put them in your phone. Text on the day: 'Glad you were born.'
When someone mentions something small last week, ask about it specifically today. 'How was the interview? How's the cat?'
Meet someone once. Use their name when you see them again weeks later. You just have a note in your phone.
When someone is telling you something difficult, lean forward physically. Not to interrupt, just to reduce the distance.
If someone tears up in public, don't ask if they're okay. Hand them a tissue. Stand closer. Let them cry without explaining.
If you see something beautiful, turn to the stranger next to you. Look at them. Look at it. Look back. Smile. Say nothing.
If someone asked you a question you couldn't answer, find the answer and tell them days later.
Carry two umbrellas. When it rains, hand one to someone without. 'Keep it.' Don't wait for return.
Carry a portable charger. Offer it to someone at 2% battery at a coffee shop.
If someone is clearly lost looking at their phone, offer directions. Then walk with them to the corner.
If you're buying coffee and someone behind you looks like they're having a day, buy theirs. Tell the cashier it's anonymous.
On public transit, stand up and walk away from your seat without eye contact. Let someone take it without the performance of gratitude.
If you see someone struggling with a bag on stairs, pick up the other end without asking. Carry it up. Keep walking.
In a parking lot, take someone's cart back after they load their car. Pretend you didn't hear when they call out.
If you share a wall with someone, knock back once when you hear them. Just once. Acknowledge their existence.
If you have a fruit tree, hang a bag of fruit on a neighbor's doorknob with a note: 'Too many. Please take.'
If your neighbor forgets trash day, drag their bin to the curb. Drag it back empty. Never mention it.
Shovel three feet of your neighbor's walk when you do yours. Just the three feet closest to you.
If a neighbor's porch light burned out, replace the bulb or leave one on their step with a note: 'For your porch.'
Instead of texting a friend, send a 30-second voice note of you just breathing or saying their name. Let them hear your alive-ness.
Send someone a link to a song or article with no explanation. Just the link. Let them discover why.
Scroll back three years in your photos. Send a friend a picture of them they don't have. 'You looked happy here.'
Text someone 'Goodnight' who you don't usually text at night. Don't explain. Let them feel thought-of.
Write a specific, detailed positive review for a small business. Name the employee if you remember.
techBoundary: Put your phone in a drawer before bed. Don't touch it until you've showered, dressed, and had a drink.
Set your phone to grayscale mode for one full day. Notice which apps lose their appeal without color psychology.
Put your phone in a sock. The friction makes checking it intentional, not a reflex. Keep it in your bag, not pocket.
Turn on airplane mode when you leave your door. Turn it off when you arrive. Notice what you observed during the dead zones.
Keep your phone in your front pocket or bag all day. Notice how many times your hand reaches for the back pocket.
Use only the phone app, texts, and maps for 24 hours. All other apps off-limits. No exceptions.
Every time you set your phone down, screen faces the surface. Picking it up requires an intentional flip. Count the flips.
Put a small piece of tape over your thumb's fingerprint sensor for one day. Unlocking becomes deliberate, not automatic.
Keep your charger across the room from your bed. The 10-foot walk to check it at night is the boundary.
Change every notification sound to the same bland tone. Remove the dopamine-specific chimes that train your reward system.
Allow yourself 10 minutes of Instagram at 7 PM only. Delete the app after. Reinstall tomorrow if needed.
Check email at 10 AM, 1 PM, 4 PM only. Set an auto-responder: 'I check email three times daily for focus.'
Log into Twitter/X but remove the ability to post for 24 hours. Break the performative loop.
No news apps or sites before noon. Your morning belongs to you, not the world's emergencies.
Watch only what you intentionally searched for on YouTube. No homepage, no recommendations, no autoplay.
Visit only the front page of one subreddit. No clicking into threads, no scrolling past page one. Surface only.
Check LinkedIn only on Sundays. Realize nothing urgent happens there.
Mute every single WhatsApp chat for 24 hours. Check manually when you choose.
Add to your Amazon cart, but no purchasing until 48 hours later. Today is browsing only.
Listen only to full albums or your own playlists on Spotify. No Discover Weekly, no Daily Mix, no Radio.
Browser gets one tab at a time. Close it before opening the next. Feel the friction of your own distraction.
Pomodoro: when the 25 minutes ends, stop for 5 even if you're in flow. Break the addiction to momentum.
Set your Slack status to 'Focusing' for 2-hour blocks. Ignore all messages. If it's urgent, they'll call. They won't call.
Close every window, tab, and document. Start from zero. Only open what you need for the next task.
One screen only for a day. No split-screen, no dual monitors. Write things down to reference them.
Empty your Downloads folder completely. Set a rule: nothing stays there overnight.
Hide your bookmark bar for 24 hours. Type URLs manually. Remember what you actually visit versus click reflexively.
Unplug your mouse, use only keyboard navigation for one work session. Feel how much scrolling is mindless.
If you need to read a long PDF, print it. No reading documents on the same screen you answer emails.
Declare email bankruptcy for the day. Archive everything older than 48 hours. If it mattered, they'll email again.
Use a physical alarm clock. Keep phone in another room all night.
No screens after sunset without blue light glasses. Notice if you actually want the content or just the light.
After 9 PM, only e-ink devices allowed. No backlit screens. Your bed becomes a different kind of space.
Unplug the TV or hide the remote. Watching requires effort. Decide if the show is worth the walk.
Everyone at the table puts phone face-down in the center. First to touch theirs does dishes. Even alone, stack your phone.
Set phone to permanent dark mode, lowest brightness, extra dim. Make the screen less appealing than the room.
Only listen to podcasts while walking outside. No sitting and consuming. Pair audio with movement or silence.
Set a 30-minute sleep timer on any video or audio. When it cuts out, don't restart. Sleep.
Post no stories for 24 hours. Break the documentation habit. Experience something without sharing it.
Scroll only, no liking, commenting, or posting for a day. Be a ghost. Notice how much energy liking takes.
Unfollow 50 accounts today. Anyone who makes you feel insufficient, anyone you don't recognize. Curate ruthlessly.
Respond to no direct messages for 24 hours. Let them sit. Notice which ones actually require immediate response.
Don't visit anyone's profile for a day. If you can't remember their handle, you don't need to see their content.
Search no hashtags, follow no trends. If you don't know why something is trending, you don't need to know today.
Write a post caption, then delete it. Post the photo with no text. Let it stand without your explanation.
Use only a flip phone or no phone for 12 hours. Carry a notebook and pen. Meet people at agreed times like it's 1998.
Do all necessary digital tasks at a library or internet cafe. The inconvenience is the boundary.
Turn off every notification, badge, and banner for 24 hours. Check apps only when you remember they exist.
Friday sundown to Saturday sundown, no screens at all. Invent your own 24-hour screen sabbath.
Write down what apps you'd use if you had only 1 hour of screen time today. Use only those. Ignore the rest.
Set an auto-responder: 'I am reducing screen time. I will respond within 48 hours. If urgent, call.' Mean it.
Keep a tally of every time you open a feed-based app. Don't judge, just count. Awareness is the first boundary.
Put all social apps in a folder named 'Later.' Move the folder to screen 3. The swipe distance is the friction.
Let your phone die. Don't charge it until morning. Experience the freedom of being unreachable by accident.
Before opening any app, state your intention out loud: 'I am opening Instagram to check my sister's post.' If you can't say it, don't open it.
